result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.is_branching()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Check if the graph is a branching (a directed forest). ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L56827-L56886){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.is_branching() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Is branching](/assets/graphs/is-branching.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Left: a directed forest of two trees, A pointing to B and C, and D pointing to E; every node has at most one incoming edge, so is_branching() returns True. Right: the same graph plus an edge from D to C (shown in the accent color); C now has two parents, A and D, so is_branching() returns False." width="100%"} A branching is a directed graph with no cycles, even when edge directions are ignored, in which every node has at most one incoming edge. Each of its weakly connected components is then an arborescence: a tree hanging from a root with all edges pointing away from it. A branching that is a single tree is an arborescence (see `is_arborescence()`), just as an undirected forest made of one tree is a tree. Branchings are what `maximum_branching()` and `minimum_branching()` return, and they model any "each item has at most one parent" structure: org charts with several heads, file systems with several roots, or the infection trees of separate outbreaks. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : `True` if the graph is a branching. Undirected and empty graphs return `False`. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} The check makes a single pass over the edges, counting in-degrees and merging the endpoints in a union-find structure: a second incoming edge, or an edge whose ends are already connected (which includes self-loops and parallel edges), rules out a branching. It runs in nearly $O(V + E)$ time. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Two separate trees, each rooted at its own node, form a branching: ::: {#7071bf61 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph(directed=True) g.add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E"]) g.add_edges([("A", "B"), ("A", "C"), ("D", "E")]) # Returns (True, False): a branching, but not a single arborescence g.is_branching(), g.is_arborescence() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (True, False) ``` ::: ::: Giving C a second parent breaks the "at most one incoming edge" rule: ::: {#00eb052d .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} g.add_edge("D", "C") g.is_branching() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` False ``` ::: :::
